analysis.one_liner: Designates the Alaska Arctic Coastal Plain as wilderness, barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the Arctic coastal plain a wilderness area never got a House floor vote; it sat in committee for two years and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would designate about 1.5 million acres of the Arctic coastal plain in Alaska as wilderness, the highest level of federal land protection. That designation closes the area to oil drilling and other development forever. It never received a vote: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, it would preserve the Arctic coastal plain's undeveloped tundra, protect caribou and other wildlife, and keep the area off-limits to oil companies. Outdoor and conservation users would keep an untouched wilderness.

how_it_helps.text: Designates roughly 1,556,793 acres of the Arctic Coastal Plain as wilderness and part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, permanently barring development there.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which would lose access to potentially oil-rich federal land in Alaska, and Alaska state interests that back development. Future energy revenue is foregone.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies and Alaska development interests

drawbacks.text: Locking up the coastal plain closes off a possibly major domestic oil reserve, which supporters of drilling argued costs jobs, revenue, and energy supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded potential oil development for permanent protection of a large, intact Arctic ecosystem. The costs fall on a concentrated industry; the benefits are diffuse and long-term.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in January 1993 and then to a subcommittee; it was never brought to a floor vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 5, 1993, by Rep. Richard Lehman with 133 cosponsors, a strongly bipartisan list of 118 Democrats and 14 Republicans.
Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on January 5, 1993, and to a subcommittee on January 26, 1993; no further action followed.
The bill died at the end of the 103rd Congress in January 1995 without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests seeking access to the coastal plain, and Alaska development supporters, benefit because the area remains open to potential drilling rather than permanently protected.

for.name: Rep. Richard H. Lehman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to designate the Arctic Coastal Plain as wilderness.

for.name: 133 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including 118 Democrats and 14 Republicans.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a vote, letting it die.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic (118 of 133), though 14 Republicans signed on, showing some bipartisan support for the bill.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently close the Arctic coastal plain to drilling, eliminating potential access for oil companies. The industry's gain would come at the cost of untouched public land.
A permanently protected wilderness supports recreation, guiding, and wildlife-dependent tourism, and preserves a public good for future users.
